title: Fact Both Ways
description: Turn one exact division over and read it from both ends, and never say either word without naming the number it belongs to.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit. With navDots the dots are controls in AI mode too: a tap on a dot starts that phase.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; Hint, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 640. One rounded card holding the key at its top right (Answer, Close, Enter, Next, or the Yes / No keys; no question bar), the working area (the whole card until Answer is tapped) and the answer drawer that slides in from the right; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 652 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it (y 656 to 892, the question and every line, printed), one small dot per phase at the right.

zones.layout: board, key only: no question bar, only its key at the right end of the top row (the question is on the bubble); the working area is the whole card (64, 108, 1472 x 520) until the child taps Answer, when the answer drawer (as tall as the working area, the key on its top row reading Close) slides in from the right
zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: Hint (data-control again), sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one small dot per phase at the footer's right (72-unit finger boxes, centred on the bubble), no text; in user AND AI mode each is a button (data-control phase-dot, data-phase k) that starts its phase

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Read one exact division from both ends at once, and learn to say what each number is a factor of, or a multiple of.
writeup.look: A turning card in the middle with both of its readings held side by side, a size rail under it and a word pad at the edge.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Fact Both Ways' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the readings written against the readings this phase has to write, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each sentence is completed with its number named and the second fixed at what the phase asks for. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The card stands in the middle of the top of the working area, 424 by 216 at 395,202, carrying one exact division written out in full. A tap turns it about its upright, one face stating the fact about factors and the other the fact about multiples, and once it has been turned both faces are lifted out and held side by side inside a single drawn frame, 880 by 216 at 167,202, with a hairline between them rather than a wall: they are one fact and the frame says so. The name it gate guards the writing bay below, 520 by 164 at 64,442: a sentence is laid out as tiles with an empty slot in it, and the word tiles reading factor and multiple will not drop until a number tile naming what they belong to has been placed. A sentence left with its slot open springs back with the slot lit and nothing marked. The size rail runs under the card, 880 by 92 at 167,442, drawn strictly to scale from nothing at its left to the greater of the two numbers at its right, with each number standing at its own distance along it and the factor slot drawn at the smaller end; a bigger number dragged into that slot is refused and the rail is redrawn at scale so that the two lengths are the whole of the explanation. The pair bay sits at the left of the lower half, 520 by 164 at 64,606, laying two numbers out as equal rows on a ruled board and returning the number they build on a card labelled as the multiple of both. The own list bay takes the right of the lower half, 500 by 164 at 616,606: one penned factor list with a wall past its last card, and beside it a track of multiples leaving the frame at the right hand edge with no end mark and no last step drawn, and one number lighting in both of them at once. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a quotient or a built number is asked for, and beside them a word pad carrying the chapter's four words, factor, multiple, finite and infinite, turned towards a partner for the flashcard quiz and answered by press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a number that divides another exactly is deep blue, a number built by multiplying is green, anything standing in both lists at once is rose, whatever is left over and any trial that fails is vermilion, the number being broken up or the total in hand is amber, and a single digit being read or added is sky blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a leftover is told by standing outside the rows before it is told by a band, and a list that stops is told by the wall at each end of it and a list that does not by the open edge of the frame. Turning the card never replaces one reading with the other. The first face stays up and the second joins it, because the moment one of the two is taken down the child is back to holding two separate things to remember instead of one fact read from either end.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last division the child turned, both of its readings still up, with the size rail drawn underneath.

phases.win: both readings stand in one frame and each names the number it belongs to
phases.does: turns the card, reads each face, and holds the two up together
phases.goal: one exact division makes a factor fact and a multiple fact at once
phases.says: Which one is the factor and which is the multiple? One division tells you both.
phases.check: 13 divides 52 exactly. Say that as a fact about factors and then as a fact about multiples, naming both numbers each time.
phases.feels: one division, and both sentences were true before either of them was written
phases.hands: Write one exact division on the board, seventy-eight divided by six is thirteen, and under it rule two lines. Have the class fill the first line with a sentence using the word factor and the second with a sentence using the word multiple, and insist that each sentence names both numbers. Then rub out the two numbers in one sentence and ask whether it still says anything at all.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which of the two numbers is doing the dividing? Second rung, the phase's: which number is being divided, and what is it to the other one? Third rung: the card is cut to a small division and the child turns it and reads both faces aloud. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the page's own wording calls a multiple the product of two or more factors and never says of what, so the word is met with nothing attached to it and is repeated back the same way.
wrong.move: says that six is a factor and stops there, without ever naming what it is a factor of.
wrong.screen: the gate holds the sentence open with its empty slot lit and nothing marked. Two further cards are laid beside it, one where six divides thirty with nothing left over and one where six is tried on twenty and two are set outside the rows, and both are read out as sentences with their numbers in. The child's half sentence stays exactly where it was built.

wrong.why: the bigger number is the one the question started from and the two words were met on the same day, so which of them attaches to which number is a coin toss.
wrong.move: writes it the other way round, calling seventy-eight a factor of six.
wrong.screen: the size rail is drawn to scale with six standing near its left hand end and seventy-eight at its right, and the factor slot at the smaller end turns the bigger number back with the two lengths left drawn. Both faces of the card are then held up in the frame together, each naming its own number, and the child's sentence stays in the writing bay beside them.

phases.screen: a card showing one exact division with both faces still blank
phases.soWhat: If one number divides another exactly, the first is a factor of the second and the second is a multiple of the first.
phases.concept: Two words for the two ends of one division

phases.win: the built number appears labelled as the multiple of both numbers in the pair
phases.does: lays the pair out as rows and reads off the number they come to
phases.goal: the product of a factor pair is the multiple those factors belong to
phases.says: These two are a pair. What is the number they build to them?
phases.check: 4 and 6 are a factor pair of 24. Write what 24 is to 4, and what it is to 6.
phases.feels: the number a pair builds belongs to both of them at once
phases.hands: Give each pair of children two number cards that multiply to something under a hundred, three and nineteen for instance, and a pile of counters. Build the rows, count the total, and write the number they built on a third card. Then ask each pair for two true sentences about their third card, one for each of the two numbers that built it.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what do those two numbers build? Second rung, the phase's: does each of them divide what they built? Third rung: the pair bay is cut to a small pair, the child lays it out and reads the total. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: fifty-seven is the number that was made, and the thing that was made is easy to hear as the thing that belongs to the two numbers that made it.
wrong.move: calls fifty-seven a factor of three and of nineteen, turning the relation the wrong way round.
wrong.screen: the pair bay lays three rows of nineteen out on the ruled board and the built card is read out as what those rows come to. The size rail is drawn under it to scale with all three numbers standing along it, and the factor slot at the smaller end takes each of the two small numbers in turn and turns the built number back. Nothing the child wrote is cleared.

wrong.why: the bigger number looks as though it did most of the work, and the smaller one reads as a multiplier rather than as a factor in its own right.
wrong.move: says the number belongs only to the bigger of the two that built it, because nineteen is nearer to fifty-seven.
wrong.screen: both divisions are run on the ruled board one under the other, fifty-seven into three rows and fifty-seven into nineteen rows, each drawn genuinely equal with the leftover shelf beside it staying empty. The two sentences are then written under their own boards, and the child's single sentence stays where it was put with its slot for the second number lit.

phases.screen: the pair bay holding two numbers with the built number still empty
phases.soWhat: The product of a factor pair is the multiple of both numbers in the pair.
phases.concept: A factor pair and the number it builds

phases.win: the bigger number is turned back on the rail and the smaller one settles in the slot
phases.does: tries the bigger number in the factor slot, then puts the smaller one in
phases.goal: a bigger number cannot be a factor of a smaller one
phases.says: Try the bigger one as the factor. Look at the rail and say what goes wrong.
phases.check: Can 96 be a factor of 12? Can 12 be a factor of 12? Say why for each.
phases.feels: the rail says it before any dividing does
phases.hands: Put thirty-five counters in one heap and twenty-one in another. Ask whether thirty-five could be a factor of twenty-one, and let somebody try to make even one row of thirty-five out of the smaller heap. Then ask whether seven is a factor of both, and build those rows too. Finish by asking whether twenty-one is a factor of twenty-one, and build that one as well.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which of the two numbers is the bigger? Second rung, the phase's: can a bigger number go into a smaller one even once? Third rung: the rail is cut to two small numbers and the child puts each of them into the factor slot in turn. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the two numbers really are connected, seven really does divide both, and a relation that exists gets attached to whichever question was asked.
wrong.move: answers yes because seven divides both of them, so the two numbers look related enough for either word.
wrong.screen: the rail is drawn to scale with seven near the left hand end and both of the others further along. Seven is dropped into the factor slot against thirty-five and settles, then against twenty-one and settles again, and the true sentence is written out for each. Thirty-five is then dropped into the factor slot against twenty-one and is turned back, with its length on the rail left drawn past the other number.

wrong.why: the half of the rule that is remembered is the half that was surprising, and less than or EQUAL TO loses its second half within a day of being read.
wrong.move: refuses to let twenty-one be a factor of twenty-one, because a factor was said to be smaller.
wrong.screen: the rail is drawn with both markers landing on exactly the same point along it, and the division runs on the board as one row holding all twenty-one with the leftover shelf beside it drawn empty and read out as empty. The rule on the word pad opens with the equal half lit, and the child's refusal stays in the answer slot beside it.

phases.screen: the size rail with two numbers on it and the factor slot waiting
phases.soWhat: A factor is never greater than the number it belongs to, though it may be equal to it.
phases.concept: A factor is never the bigger one

phases.win: the same number lights at the closed end of the pen and at the start of the track
phases.does: drops one number into both lists and reads where it lands in each
phases.goal: a number is its own greatest factor and its own smallest multiple
phases.says: Put it in both lists. Where does it sit in one, and where in the other?
phases.check: Where does 44 stand in its own list of factors, and where in its own list of multiples?
phases.feels: the same number shuts one list and opens the other
phases.hands: Take seventeen and write its factors on one side of the board and the first few of its multiples on the other, leaving the multiple list open with nothing after the last one. Ask a child to ring the same number in both lists. Then do it again with forty-four, which has six factors rather than two, and ask whether the ringed number moved.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which number is standing at the shut end of the pen? Second rung, the phase's: which number is the first step of the track? Third rung: the bay is cut to a small number, the child fills both lists and rings what stands in each. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: a list of a number's factors is heard as a list of the numbers that go into it, and a thing is not usually counted among the things that make it up.
wrong.move: leaves the number out of both of its own lists, because its own lists sound like lists of other numbers.
wrong.screen: the own list bay lights the shut end of the pen and the first step of the track at the same instant, with the same number card standing in each. The two claims are then run in front of the child: the number divided by itself, drawn as one row with nothing outside it, and one step of the number, drawn landing on it. The child's two lists stay exactly as they were written.

wrong.why: the whole chapter has been setting the two words against each other, one list closing in and the other running out, so a number standing in both reads as a contradiction rather than as the place where they meet.
wrong.move: says a number cannot be in both lists at once, because factor and multiple sound like opposites, and drops it from whichever was written second.
wrong.screen: the pen and the track are drawn side by side with the number lit in both and a hairline joining the two marks. The pen is read from its left post to its wall, ending on the number, and the track is read from its first step outward, starting on the number and leaving the frame. Nothing is removed from either list.

phases.screen: the own list bay with a penned factor list and a running track side by side
phases.soWhat: A number is its own greatest factor and its own smallest multiple.
phases.concept: A number stands at both ends of its own list

writeup.delight: The first phase, at the turn. The card goes over once and the two faces do not take turns: the first one lifts clear and slides to the left of the frame while the second rises into the right of it, and for the length of that movement the division itself is drawn joining them, the same numbers running through both sentences. Drag either reading and the other comes with it, hinged, because neither was found without the other. Try to lift one out of the frame on its own and it will not come, and the hairline between the two lights instead of any warning being spoken.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase one exact division stands on the card in the middle of the stage with both of its written faces still blank and the frame beside it empty and ruled for two. On the second the pair bay holds two numbers with the ruled board between them bare and the built number still an empty card. On the third the size rail is drawn to scale with two numbers standing along it and the factor slot at its smaller end waiting. On the fourth the own list bay is open with a penned factor list on the left, both of its walls up, and a track of multiples on the right leaving the frame with no end mark, and one number card lying between them. The running count at the top left holds the readings written against the readings this phase has to write, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the card, or the empty built number, or the factor slot, or the number card lying between the two lists, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks which of the two numbers is the one doing the dividing. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any exact division on the card, with the size rail live, the pair bay open and the word pad turned towards a partner. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on naming which number is the factor and which the multiple, building a number from a pair, refusing a factor bigger than its number, and finding the number that closes one list and opens the other.
voiceLines: One division on a card. It has another face, and both of them are true.
Which one is the factor and which is the multiple? One division tells you both.
These two are a pair. What is the number they build to them?
Try the bigger one as the factor. Look at the rail and say what goes wrong.
Put it in both lists. Where does it sit in one, and where in the other?
A new division on the card. Read it from one end, then from the other.
Free play. Any exact division on the card, the rail live, the word pad turned over.
Say it again, and this time say which number it belongs to.
Every card turned, and never once a word left hanging with no number on it.

observations.why: Dividing exactly is one relation between two numbers, and the two words simply name its two ends.
observations.soWhat: Knowing that one number divides another is already knowing both facts.
observations.observe: One division produced two sentences and no second piece of work was done for the second one.

observations.why: A number is a factor of something and a multiple of something, so the word on its own says nothing at all.
observations.soWhat: Always say what a number is a factor of, or a multiple of.
observations.observe: Neither word would go into a sentence until a number had been named for it.

observations.why: A factor has to go into the number, and a number bigger than it cannot go in even once.
observations.soWhat: A factor is never greater than the number it belongs to, though it may be equal to it.
observations.observe: The rail turned the bigger number back every time it was offered as the factor.

observations.why: A number divides itself exactly, and one step of it lands on itself.
observations.soWhat: A number is its own greatest factor and its own smallest multiple.
observations.observe: The same number lit at the shut end of one list and at the first step of the other.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The rail draws both numbers to scale and the smaller one hops along it, landing exactly on the bigger; then both faces of the card stand up together, each naming its number.
Phase 2: The rows are laid out again one at a time and counted at their ends, and the built card is named for both numbers of the pair.
Phase 3: The rail offers each number to the factor slot in turn: a smaller one settles, a bigger one is turned back with its extra length left drawn.
Phase 4: The number stands at the shut end of its pen and the first step of its track at once, a hairline joins the two, and each list is read up to it.

voice.opening: One division on a card. It has another face, and both of them are true.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play: turn any card, hop along the rail, and try a new card.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs, shown at once UNDER the pinned instruction and kept until the child acts again
voice.onFinish: Every card turned, and never once a word left hanging with no number on it.
voice.rules: Silent: nothing is spoken (no device speech, no recorded clips, no Tap to start cover). The speech bubble is the guide: every instruction and hint is one printed page, numbers as words. The lesson is action-driven in every mode: a guide step's instruction stays until the child does the act it names; a wrong act shows that step's hint under the pinned instruction, a wrong answer the next rung of its ladder, and the hint stays unchanged until the child acts again; a right answer's next question, a phase's next phase and the summary's rows follow by themselves after a short celebration. The header's Hint key shows the step's hint or the next rung on demand. What is heard is sound effects (Web Audio), switched by the sound button, on in every mode. In classroom mode nothing waits for a tap except the pieces of a long line (the blinking arrow; a tap, Enter, Space, ArrowRight or PageDown on the bubble shows the next piece), and a tap on the bubble when nothing waits is the teacher's skip.

guide.playsOn: guide steps on phase 1, 2, 3, 4: the phase opens on its first instruction and waits for the child's act (getState guideStep, guideSteps, guideOn); the agent's check() performs the current step; the last act opens the first question. Other phases open on their printed teach lines, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: 6 divides 78 exactly. Which of the two is the factor and which is the multiple?

question.en: 6 divides 78 exactly, so which number is the factor of which?

items.planAnswer: 6 is a factor of 78, and 78 is a multiple of 6

items.planQuestion: 7 divides 77 exactly. Say that as a fact about factors and as a fact about multiples.

question.en: Which number is the multiple here, since 7 divides 77 exactly?

items.planAnswer: 7 is a factor of 77, and 77 is a multiple of 7

items.planQuestion: In the multiplication 8 times 9 is 72, which number is the multiple?

question.en: In the multiplication 8 times 9 is 72, which number is the multiple?

items.planQuestion: 2 and 23 are a factor pair. Which number do they build, and what is it to them?

question.en: 2 and 23 are a factor pair, so which number do they build?

items.planAnswer: 46, and 46 is a multiple of both 2 and 23

items.planQuestion: 3 and 19 are a factor pair of 57. What is 57 to them?

question.en: 3 and 19 are a factor pair of 57, so what is 57 to them?

items.planAnswer: Their multiple: 57 is a multiple of 3 and a multiple of 19

items.planQuestion: Write all three factor pairs of 20, and say what 20 is to each pair.

question.en: Find the factor pairs of 20 by tapping the numbers that fit.

items.planAnswer: 1 and 20, 2 and 10, and 4 and 5. 20 is the multiple of every one of those pairs
No. 88 is greater than 44, and a factor is never greater than the number it divides. 44 is a factor of 88 instead

items.planQuestion: A child says 9 is a factor of 6, because 3 divides both of them. What is wrong, and what is true?

question.en: Which number is a factor of both 6 and 9?

items.planAnswer: 9 is greater than 6, so it cannot divide 6 exactly. What is true is that 3 is a factor of both 6 and 9

items.planQuestion: Where does 17 sit in its own list of factors, and in its own list of multiples?

question.en: Where does 17 belong: in its factors, in its multiples, or in both?

items.planAnswer: At the top of one and the foot of the other: 17 is the greatest factor of 17 and the smallest multiple of 17

items.planQuestion: Name the greatest factor of 34 and the smallest multiple of 34.

question.en: Name the greatest factor of 34 and the smallest multiple of 34.

items.planQuestion: Which number is both the greatest factor of 65 and its smallest multiple, and what are all four of its factors?

question.en: Tap every factor of 65 into the pen, then press Enter.

items.planAnswer: 65 itself, and its factors are 1, 5, 13 and 65

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page (a tool with nextKey, runtime r48+: in user mode it waits for the child's blinking Next key instead, after every question and every phase, and the last phase's key opens the summary; AI mode, and a host that mounts one phase without navigableDots, walk on by themselves); finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }

phases.concept: Two words for the two ends of one division
A factor pair and the number it builds
A factor is never the bigger one
A number stands at both ends of its own list

getState: toolId, mediaId, mode, mountPhase, phase, phases, conceptId, objectiveIds, step, steps, item, items, stage (teach, demo, ask, win, idle, summary, free), question, questionText, choices, typed, keypadOpen, tries, answered, firstTry, score, maxScore, answerShown (only after the answer), complete, questionCount, muted (the sound effects), speaking (always false: the lesson is silent), voice ("silent"), mascot, summaryRow, played, classroom, held (a classroom's parked piece of a long line), instruction (the pinned line), hint (the hint under it, or null), guideStep / guideSteps / guideOn (a guide-steps phase only), division, faceUp, turned, bothHeld, namedNumber, x, railOrder, builtNumber, complete

terminalEvent.name: finished
terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first

sounds: Web Audio, no files, on in every mode (the sound button switches them): correct, wrong (soft), win at a phase end, cheer at the last, a tick when a piece snaps, and cut, settle and trade where the picture moves

voiceLines.en: One division on a card. It has another face, and both of them are true.
Which one is the factor and which is the multiple? One division tells you both.
These two are a pair. What is the number they build to them?
Try the bigger one as the factor. Look at the rail and say what goes wrong.
Put it in both lists. Where does it sit in one, and where in the other?
A new division on the card. Read it from one end, then from the other.
Free play. Any exact division on the card, the rail live, the word pad turned over.
Say it again, and this time say which number it belongs to.
Every card turned, and never once a word left hanging with no number on it.
